_about: Background for the Sikh History day pages (scripts/build-sikh-history-pages.js). 'eras' give the historical setting for an event by its year; 'entities' are the people, places, institutions and movements the events mention (matched by the 'match' patterns, case-insensitive), each with a short summary, a page on this site and, where useful, a public-domain historical image. Edit here, then re-run the build script.

eras.name: Before the Guru period
eras.text: Events before 1469 belong to the world into which Sikhism was born: Punjab under the Delhi Sultanate and successive Afghan and Turkic rulers, and the Bhakti and Sufi movements whose saints' verses were later included in the Guru Granth Sahib.

eras.name: The early Gurus (1469–1605)
eras.text: Guru Nanak Dev Ji (1469–1539) founded the Sikh faith, travelled widely and settled the first Sikh community at Kartarpur. His successors built its institutions: Guru Angad Dev Ji standardised the Gurmukhi script, Guru Amar Das Ji organised the sangat into manjis and made langar central, Guru Ram Das Ji founded the town of Ramdaspur (Amritsar), and Guru Arjan Dev Ji built Sri Harmandir Sahib and compiled the Adi Granth in 1604.

eras.name: Miri-Piri and the middle Gurus (1606–1674)
eras.text: After the martyrdom of Guru Arjan Dev Ji in 1606, Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji wore two swords of miri and piri (temporal and spiritual authority), established the Akal Takht and fought several engagements with Mughal forces. The seventh and eighth Gurus, Guru Har Rai Ji and Guru Har Krishan Ji, led the community from Kiratpur and Delhi, and Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji founded Anandpur (Chak Nanaki) in 1665.

eras.name: Guru Gobind Singh Ji and the Khalsa (1675–1708)
eras.text: Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji was executed in Delhi in 1675 on Aurangzeb's orders, and his son Guru Gobind Singh Ji became the tenth Guru at the age of nine. From Anandpur and Paonta he led the Sikhs through conflicts with the hill rajas and Mughal governors, created the Khalsa at Vaisakhi in 1699, and in the battles of 1704–1705 lost all four Sahibzade. Before his death at Nanded in 1708 he vested Guruship in the Guru Granth Sahib and the Khalsa Panth.

eras.name: Banda Singh Bahadur (1709–1716)
eras.text: Sent north by Guru Gobind Singh Ji, Banda Singh Bahadur led a Sikh uprising that captured Samana and, in 1710, Sirhind, ending the rule of Wazir Khan. He set up Sikh rule from Mukhlisgarh (Lohgarh), issued coins in the name of the Gurus and abolished the zamindari system in the areas he held, before being besieged at Gurdas Nangal and executed in Delhi in 1716.

eras.name: Persecution, the Dal Khalsa and Abdali's invasions (1717–1764)
eras.text: After Banda Singh's death the Mughal governors of Lahore, notably Zakariya Khan and Mir Mannu, put prices on Sikh heads, and many Sikhs, such as Bhai Mani Singh and Bhai Taru Singh, were executed. The Sikhs organised in jathas, united as the Dal Khalsa in 1748 and resisted the repeated invasions of Ahmad Shah Abdali, who killed thousands of Sikhs in the Vadda Ghallughara of 1762 and blew up Sri Harmandir Sahib, which the Sikhs rebuilt.

eras.name: The Misl period (1765–1798)
eras.text: From 1765, when the Sikhs took Lahore and struck their own coins, Punjab was held by twelve Sikh confederacies, the misls, led by sardars such as Jassa Singh Ahluwalia, Jassa Singh Ramgarhia and the Bhangi and Sukerchakia chiefs. They met as the Sarbat Khalsa at Amritsar and extended Sikh power from the Indus towards Delhi.

eras.name: The Sikh Empire of Maharaja Ranjit Singh (1799–1839)
eras.text: Ranjit Singh of the Sukerchakia misl took Lahore in 1799, was proclaimed Maharaja in 1801 and united the misls into a single state stretching from Peshawar and Kashmir to the Sutlej. He modernised the Khalsa army, gilded Sri Harmandir Sahib, and kept peace with the British under the Treaty of Amritsar (1809).

eras.name: Decline of the Lahore Darbar and annexation (1840–1849)
eras.text: After Ranjit Singh's death in 1839, the Lahore Darbar was torn by the murders of three successive rulers and court intrigue under the Dogra ministers. The First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–46) and the Second (1848–49) ended with the British annexation of Punjab in 1849 and the exile of the young Maharaja Duleep Singh.

eras.name: Colonial Punjab and the Singh Sabha revival (1850–1919)
eras.text: Under British rule Sikhs were recruited in large numbers into the army while new reform movements arose: the Namdhari (Kuka) movement, the Singh Sabha movement founded at Amritsar in 1873, the Chief Khalsa Diwan (1902), Khalsa College and the Anand Marriage Act (1909). The period ended with the Ghadar movement, the Komagata Maru episode (1914) and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 13 April 1919.

eras.name: The Gurdwara Reform (Akali) movement (1920–1925)
eras.text: Sikhs organised the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (November 1920) and the Shiromani Akali Dal (December 1920) to free historic gurdwaras from hereditary mahants backed by the government. Through non-violent morchas, including Nankana Sahib (1921), the keys agitation (1921–22), Guru ka Bagh (1922) and Jaito (1923–25), and alongside the militant Babbar Akali movement, the campaign led to the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925.

eras.name: Late colonial Punjab and Partition (1926–1947)
eras.text: With the SGPC established by law, Sikh politics was led by the Akali Dal under figures such as Master Tara Singh and Baba Kharak Singh. Sikhs took part in the freedom movement and in both World Wars, and the Partition of Punjab in August 1947 divided the Sikh homeland, leaving Nankana Sahib and many historic shrines in Pakistan and uprooting millions of Sikhs.

eras.name: The Punjabi Suba movement (1948–1966)
eras.text: In independent India the Akali Dal campaigned for a Punjabi-speaking state, the Punjabi Suba, through repeated morchas led by Master Tara Singh and Sant Fateh Singh. The demand was met with the reorganisation of Punjab on 1 November 1966, which created present-day Punjab, Haryana and transferred hill areas to Himachal Pradesh.

eras.name: From the Anandpur Sahib Resolution to 1984 (1967–1984)
eras.text: The Akali Dal adopted the Anandpur Sahib Resolution in 1973 and launched the Dharam Yudh Morcha in 1982 over river waters, Chandigarh and greater state autonomy. Tensions culminated in Operation Blue Star, the Indian Army's assault on the Darbar Sahib complex in June 1984, the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi on 31 October 1984 and the anti-Sikh violence in Delhi and elsewhere that followed.

eras.name: Since 1985
eras.text: The years after 1984 saw the Rajiv–Longowal Accord (1985), a decade of militancy and counter-insurgency in Punjab, and the growth of a large Sikh diaspora. More recent milestones include the 300th anniversary of the Khalsa in 1999 and the opening of the Kartarpur Corridor in 2019.

entities.name: Guru Nanak Dev Ji
entities.summary: The founder of Sikhism (1469–1539), born at Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib. He taught devotion to one Creator, honest work and sharing, travelled across South Asia and beyond on his udasis, and spent his last years at Kartarpur on the Ravi.

entities.name: Guru Angad Dev Ji
entities.summary: The second Guru (1504–1552), formerly Bhai Lehna. From Khadur Sahib he gave the Gurmukhi script its standard form, collected Guru Nanak's hymns and encouraged physical fitness and langar.

entities.name: Guru Amar Das Ji
entities.summary: The third Guru (1479–1574), who made Goindwal a centre of the faith with its baoli, organised the sangat into 22 manjis, insisted that all visitors eat together in langar and spoke against purdah and sati.

entities.name: Guru Ram Das Ji
entities.summary: The fourth Guru (1534–1581), formerly Bhai Jetha and husband of Bibi Bhani. He founded the town of Ramdaspur, later Amritsar, began excavating its sacred pool and composed the Lavan used in the Sikh wedding ceremony.

entities.name: Guru Arjan Dev Ji
entities.summary: The fifth Guru (1563–1606), who built Sri Harmandir Sahib, founded Tarn Taran and Kartarpur (Jalandhar), and compiled the Adi Granth in 1604. He was tortured to death in Lahore in 1606, the first Sikh martyr Guru.

entities.name: Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji
entities.summary: The sixth Guru (1595–1644), who wore the swords of miri and piri, built the Akal Takht in 1606, was held in Gwalior Fort and released with 52 rajas (remembered as Bandi Chhor Diwas), and fought several battles with Mughal forces before settling at Kiratpur.

entities.name: Guru Har Rai Ji
entities.summary: The seventh Guru (1630–1661), who led the Sikhs from Kiratpur, kept a large mounted force and was known for his compassion and his herbal dispensary.

entities.name: Guru Har Krishan Ji
entities.summary: The eighth Guru (1656–1664), who became Guru at the age of five and died in Delhi of smallpox after tending the sick there; Gurdwara Bangla Sahib marks the place where he stayed.

entities.name: Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji
entities.summary: The ninth Guru (1621–1675), recognised at Bakala by the trader Makhan Shah Lubana. He founded Anandpur, travelled as far as Assam, and was executed in Chandni Chowk, Delhi, in 1675 for defending religious freedom; Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib marks the spot.

entities.name: Guru Gobind Singh Ji
entities.summary: The tenth Guru (1666–1708), born at Patna. He created the Khalsa in 1699, led the Sikhs through the battles of Anandpur, Chamkaur and Muktsar, composed works collected in the Dasam Granth, and before his death at Nanded vested Guruship in the Guru Granth Sahib.

entities.name: Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji
entities.summary: The Sikh scripture and eternal Guru. Compiled by Guru Arjan Dev Ji as the Adi Granth and installed at Sri Harmandir Sahib in 1604, it was completed with the hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji at Damdama Sahib and given Guruship by Guru Gobind Singh Ji in 1708.

entities.name: The Sahibzade
entities.summary: The four sons of Guru Gobind Singh Ji. The elder two, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, fell at Chamkaur in December 1704; the younger two, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, were bricked in alive at Sirhind on the orders of Wazir Khan, an event remembered every December during Shaheedi Jor Mela.

entities.name: Baba Buddha Ji
entities.summary: A disciple of Guru Nanak Dev Ji who lived through the time of six Gurus (c. 1506–1631). He performed the tilak ceremony for the second to sixth Gurus and was the first granthi of Sri Harmandir Sahib.

entities.name: Bhai Gurdas Ji
entities.summary: A scholar and poet (c. 1551–1636), a relative of Guru Amar Das Ji, who acted as scribe when Guru Arjan Dev Ji compiled the Adi Granth. His Vaaran are called the key to the Guru Granth Sahib.

entities.name: Baba Banda Singh Bahadur
entities.summary: The general (1670–1716) sent to Punjab by Guru Gobind Singh Ji. He captured Sirhind in 1710, set up the first Sikh rule with its capital at Lohgarh and ended the zamindari system in the lands he held, before being captured at Gurdas Nangal and executed in Delhi in 1716.

entities.name: Bhai Mani Singh Ji
entities.summary: A companion of Guru Gobind Singh Ji and later head granthi of Sri Harmandir Sahib. He wrote out a recension of the Guru Granth Sahib and was executed in Lahore by being cut limb from limb for refusing to give up his faith.

entities.name: Bhai Taru Singh Ji
entities.summary: A young Sikh of Poolha village who helped feed Sikhs in hiding. Arrested under Zakariya Khan, he refused to cut his hair and had his scalp removed in Lahore in 1745; he is remembered as an example of steadfast faith.

entities.name: Baba Deep Singh Ji
entities.summary: A scholar-warrior (1682–1757) and head of the Shaheedan misl who made copies of the Guru Granth Sahib at Damdama Sahib. He died in 1757 fighting Afghan forces to free Sri Harmandir Sahib from desecration; Gurdwara Shaheedan Sahib in Amritsar marks the spot.

entities.name: Ahmad Shah Abdali
entities.summary: The founder of the Durrani Empire of Afghanistan (c. 1722–1772), who invaded India repeatedly from 1747 to 1767. His campaigns against the Sikhs included the Vadda Ghallughara of February 1762 and the destruction of Sri Harmandir Sahib, but Sikh resistance prevented him from holding Punjab.

entities.name: Mughal rulers and governors
entities.summary: The Mughal emperors Jahangir and Aurangzeb ordered the executions of Guru Arjan Dev Ji and Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji, and Aurangzeb's successors and the governors of Lahore and Sirhind, among them Wazir Khan, Zakariya Khan and Mir Mannu, led the long campaign against the Sikhs between 1704 and the 1750s.

entities.name: The misl sardars
entities.summary: The leaders of the Sikh confederacies of the 18th century, such as Nawab Kapur Singh, Jassa Singh Ahluwalia, Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, Baghel Singh and Baba Ala Singh of Patiala. Organised as the Dal Khalsa, they resisted the Afghans and in 1783 Baghel Singh's forces entered Delhi and marked the Sikh historical sites there.

entities.name: Maharaja Ranjit Singh
entities.summary: The founder of the Sikh Empire (1780–1839). He took Lahore in 1799, was proclaimed Maharaja in 1801, unified the misls, built a modern army, and covered Sri Harmandir Sahib in gold, giving it the name Golden Temple.

entities.name: Hari Singh Nalwa
entities.summary: Commander-in-chief of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's army (1791–1837), who extended the Sikh Empire to Kashmir, Peshawar and the Khyber and died defending Jamrud in 1837.

entities.name: Akali Phula Singh
entities.summary: A Nihang leader and jathedar of the Akal Takht (1761–1823) who commanded troops for Maharaja Ranjit Singh and fell at the battle of Naushera in 1823.

entities.name: The Lahore Darbar after Ranjit Singh
entities.summary: The court at Lahore after 1839, when Kharak Singh, Nau Nihal Singh and Sher Singh ruled in quick succession and the Dogra ministers Dhian Singh, Hira Singh and Gulab Singh competed for power. Under Maharani Jind Kaur the Khalsa army fought the British in two Anglo-Sikh wars, which ended in annexation in 1849.

entities.name: Maharaja Duleep Singh
entities.summary: The last Maharaja of the Sikh Empire (1838–1893), youngest son of Ranjit Singh. Deposed at the age of ten when Punjab was annexed in 1849, he was taken to England, later tried to return to India and reclaim his heritage, and died in Paris.

entities.name: Bhai Maharaj Singh
entities.summary: A Sikh saint-soldier who led resistance to British rule after the Anglo-Sikh wars. Captured in 1849, he was deported to Singapore in 1850 and died in prison there in 1856.

entities.name: The Namdhari (Kuka) movement
entities.summary: A reform movement led by Baba Ram Singh from Bhaini Sahib, which boycotted British goods, courts and schools. After the Kukas' attack on Malerkotla in 1872, dozens were blown from guns without trial and Baba Ram Singh was exiled to Burma.

entities.name: The Singh Sabha movement
entities.summary: A Sikh revival movement begun with the founding of the Sri Guru Singh Sabha at Amritsar in 1873, followed by the Lahore Singh Sabha and the Khalsa Diwans. It promoted Sikh education, Punjabi literature and Sikh rites, led to Khalsa College, Amritsar (1892), the Chief Khalsa Diwan (1902) and the Anand Marriage Act (1909).

entities.name: The Ghadar movement and Komagata Maru
entities.summary: An anti-colonial movement founded in 1913 by Indian, largely Punjabi Sikh, emigrants in North America. In 1914 the ship Komagata Maru (renamed Guru Nanak Jahaz), chartered by Baba Gurdit Singh, was refused entry to Canada and fired upon at Budge Budge on its return; the planned Ghadar uprising of 1915 was crushed.

entities.name: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre
entities.summary: On Vaisakhi, 13 April 1919, troops under Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer fired without warning on an unarmed crowd in the Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar, killing hundreds. The massacre turned many Indians, including Sikhs, against British rule.

entities.name: The SGPC
entities.summary: The Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, formed at a meeting at the Akal Takht in November 1920 to manage historic gurdwaras, and given legal standing by the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925. It manages Sri Harmandir Sahib and gurdwaras in Punjab, Himachal Pradesh and Chandigarh.

entities.name: The Akali movement and its morchas
entities.summary: The Gurdwara Reform movement of 1920–1925, in which jathas of Akali volunteers non-violently took control of historic gurdwaras from mahants. Its campaigns included the keys morcha, Guru ka Bagh and Jaito; tens of thousands were arrested and hundreds killed or injured before the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925. The Shiromani Akali Dal has remained the main Sikh political party.

entities.name: Nankana Sahib and the Saka of 1921
entities.summary: Nankana Sahib, near Lahore, is the birthplace of Guru Nanak Dev Ji. On 20 February 1921 over a hundred Sikhs of a peaceful jatha led by Bhai Lachhman Singh Dharowalia were killed at Gurdwara Janam Asthan by men of Mahant Narain Das, one of the defining events of the Gurdwara Reform movement. Since 1947 it lies in Pakistan.

image.alt: Gurdwara Janam Asthan, Nankana Sahib, in 1932
image.caption: Gurdwara Janam Asthan, Nankana Sahib, photographed on 4 July 1932 by the pilgrim Bhai Dhanna Singh Chahal 'Patialvi'.
image.credit: Dhanna Singh Chahal, 1932 · Panjab Digital Library via Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

entities.name: The Jaito Morcha
entities.summary: An Akali campaign of 1923–1925, begun after an akhand path at Gurdwara Gangsar, Jaito, was interrupted during agitation over the forced abdication of Maharaja Ripudaman Singh of Nabha. Shahidi jathas of 500 marched to Jaito; on 21 February 1924 the first jatha was fired on near the gurdwara, and the morcha ended when the akhand path was completed in 1925.

entities.name: The Babbar Akalis
entities.summary: A militant group of 1921–1925 in the Doaba region, led by figures such as Kishan Singh Gargaj, who rejected the Akalis' non-violence and targeted officials and informers. Several of its leaders were hanged in 1926; the SGPC disowned its methods in 1923.

entities.name: Baba Kharak Singh
entities.summary: The first president of the SGPC (1868–1963), who led the keys morcha and was imprisoned many times by the British; Gandhi hailed the return of the Darbar Sahib keys in 1922 as the first decisive victory of the freedom struggle.

entities.name: Master Tara Singh
entities.summary: The leading Akali politician of the mid-20th century (1885–1967). He headed the Akali Dal and SGPC for decades, represented the Sikhs in the negotiations before Partition and led the early Punjabi Suba campaigns.

entities.name: The Punjabi Suba movement
entities.summary: The campaign of 1947–1966 for a Punjabi-speaking state, led by the Akali Dal under Master Tara Singh and Sant Fateh Singh, with mass morchas in 1955 and 1960–61. It succeeded when Punjab was reorganised on 1 November 1966; Darshan Singh Pheruman died on a fast in 1969 over the transfer of Chandigarh.

entities.name: The Partition of 1947
entities.summary: The division of British India in August 1947 split Punjab between India and Pakistan. Hundreds of thousands were killed in the communal violence, millions of Sikhs and Hindus left West Punjab, and Nankana Sahib, Kartarpur, Panja Sahib and Lahore's Sikh shrines were left in Pakistan.

entities.name: The Anandpur Sahib Resolution
entities.summary: A statement of Akali aims adopted at Anandpur Sahib in 1973, calling for greater autonomy for Punjab, which became the basis of the Dharam Yudh Morcha of 1982–84 and of the Rajiv–Longowal Accord of 1985; Sant Harchand Singh Longowal was assassinated weeks after signing the accord.

entities.name: Operation Blue Star and November 1984
entities.summary: In June 1984 the Indian Army attacked the Darbar Sahib complex in Amritsar and some forty other gurdwaras to remove armed militants led by Sant Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale; many pilgrims were killed and the Akal Takht was heavily damaged. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated by her Sikh bodyguards on 31 October 1984, and thousands of Sikhs were killed in the violence that followed in Delhi and other cities.

entities.name: Sri Harmandir Sahib (Darbar Sahib)
entities.summary: The central Sikh shrine in Amritsar, built by Guru Arjan Dev Ji in the middle of the sacred pool, where the Adi Granth was installed in 1604. Destroyed by Ahmad Shah Abdali and rebuilt, it was covered in gold under Maharaja Ranjit Singh and has been at the centre of many events in Sikh history.

image.alt: Sri Harmandir Sahib photographed by Felice Beato, about 1858–1860
image.caption: Sri Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar, in one of the earliest photographs of the shrine, about 1858–1860.
image.credit: Felice Beato · V&A collection via Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

entities.name: Sri Akal Takht Sahib
entities.summary: The highest seat of Sikh temporal authority, facing Sri Harmandir Sahib, founded by Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji in 1606. Decisions of the Sarbat Khalsa and hukamnamas binding on the Panth are issued from here.

entities.name: Amritsar
entities.summary: The city founded by Guru Ram Das Ji around the sacred pool of Amritsar. As the home of Sri Harmandir Sahib and the Akal Takht it has been the spiritual and political centre of the Sikhs for four centuries.

image.alt: The causeway to Sri Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar, in 1870
image.caption: The causeway to the sanctum of Sri Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar, in 1870.
image.credit: William Henry Baker, 1870 · British Library via Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

entities.name: Lahore
entities.summary: The historic capital of Punjab, where Guru Arjan Dev Ji was martyred (Gurdwara Dera Sahib) and Maharaja Ranjit Singh ruled the Sikh Empire from the Lahore Fort. After 1947 it became part of Pakistan.

image.alt: Lahore Fort photographed by Samuel Bourne in the 1860s
image.caption: The Lahore Fort, seat of the Sikh Empire, photographed in the 1860s.
image.credit: Samuel Bourne, 1860s · via Wikipedia · Public domain

entities.name: Anandpur Sahib
entities.summary: The town founded by Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji in 1665 as Chak Nanaki, where Guru Gobind Singh Ji created the Khalsa at Vaisakhi in 1699. Takht Sri Keshgarh Sahib stands there, and the town hosts Hola Mohalla every year.

entities.name: Chamkaur Sahib
entities.summary: The site of the battle of December 1704 in which Guru Gobind Singh Ji, with forty Sikhs, held a mud fortress against a far larger Mughal force; the two elder Sahibzade, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, fell here.

image.alt: Gurdwara Garhi Sahib, Chamkaur Sahib, in the 1920s
image.caption: Gurdwara Garhi Sahib at Chamkaur Sahib in the 1920s, as published in the Mahan Kosh (1930).
image.credit: Kahn Singh Nabha, Mahan Kosh · via Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

entities.name: Sirhind (Fatehgarh Sahib)
entities.summary: The Mughal provincial town where the younger Sahibzade were executed in December 1704; Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib marks the site. Banda Singh Bahadur captured Sirhind in 1710, and the Dal Khalsa took and razed it in 1764.

entities.name: Sri Muktsar Sahib
entities.summary: The site of the battle of Khidrana in 1705, where forty Sikhs led by Mai Bhago fought the pursuing Mughal army; Guru Gobind Singh Ji blessed them as the Chali Mukte, the forty liberated ones, remembered each year at Maghi.

entities.name: Takht Sri Damdama Sahib
entities.summary: At Talwandi Sabo, where Guru Gobind Singh Ji stayed in 1705–06 and the final recension of the Guru Granth Sahib was prepared. It was recognised as the fifth Takht of the Sikhs in the 20th century.

entities.name: Takht Sri Patna Sahib
entities.summary: At Patna in Bihar, the birthplace of Guru Gobind Singh Ji in 1666 and one of the five Takhts.

entities.name: Takht Sri Hazur Sahib, Nanded
entities.summary: At Nanded on the Godavari, where Guru Gobind Singh Ji spent his last days, met Banda Singh Bahadur and in 1708 vested Guruship in the Guru Granth Sahib. Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib stands there.

entities.name: Kiratpur Sahib
entities.summary: The town on the Sutlej founded in the time of Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, where the sixth and seventh Gurus lived and where Sikhs immerse the ashes of their dead at Patalpuri.

entities.name: Goindwal and Khadur Sahib
entities.summary: Neighbouring towns on the Beas. Khadur Sahib was the seat of Guru Angad Dev Ji and Goindwal that of Guru Amar Das Ji, who built its baoli with 84 steps.

entities.name: Kartarpur
entities.summary: Two places share the name: Kartarpur on the Ravi, now in Pakistan, founded by Guru Nanak Dev Ji, who lived and died there (the Kartarpur Corridor opened in 2019); and Kartarpur near Jalandhar, founded by Guru Arjan Dev Ji.

entities.name: Delhi
entities.summary: The Mughal capital, where Guru Har Krishan Ji died (Gurdwara Bangla Sahib), Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji was executed (Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib) and Banda Singh Bahadur was put to death in 1716. Baghel Singh's forces entered the city in 1783 and marked its Sikh sites.

entities.name: The Khalsa Panth
entities.summary: The order of initiated Sikhs created by Guru Gobind Singh Ji at Anandpur Sahib on Vaisakhi 1699, when the Panj Pyare were the first to receive amrit. With the Guru Granth Sahib, the Khalsa Panth carries the Guru's authority.
